title: A 38Mb/mm2 380/540mV Dual-Rail SRAM in 3nm-FinFET Technology
problem: Ultra-low-voltage SRAM design faces fundamental challenge: bitcell array requires minimum voltage (V_DDA) for read/write stability, while shared SoC logic operates at lower standard supply voltage (V_DD). Large voltage gap forces conventional level-shifter overhead, increasing area and power. 3nm technology enables high density but demands voltage flexibility for extreme-low-power SoC applications.
motivation: Energy-critical systems (mobile, IoT, edge AI) benefit from lowest-possible SoC logic voltage; SRAM must not constrain this optimization. Achieving lowest V_DD without sacrificing SRAM yield and functionality is critical.
method: Conventional SRAM designs force the entire chip to operate at the voltage the memory cells need, even if logic around it could run lower and save power. This design decouples that using Interface Dual-Rail (IDR): the SRAM interface runs at ultra-low voltage (380mV minimum—the lowest reported for this memory type), while internal cells stay at their required higher voltage. An extended-range level shifter (a converter with built-in latches) and a bypass path on the clock signal handle the voltage conversion with minimal overhead. The chip's main logic can now operate independently of memory voltage needs, achieving 38 megabits per square millimeter density—the highest reported for single-port SRAM.
key_novelty: Decoupling SRAM interface voltage from internal cell voltage using an extended-range level shifter to enable 380mV ultra-low-voltage operation.
contributions: Extended-range level shifter (ERLS) with minimal area overhead
baselines: conventional dual-rail SRAM with standard level-shifters
limitations: Abstract does not discuss access time, read/write latency, power consumption per access, leakage at 380mV, yield data, or comparison with distributed low-voltage SRAM schemes.
primary_theme: interface-decoupled ultra-low-voltage SRAM with extended-range level-shifter
